avatar.question: Are you real? How does this avatar work?
avatar.answer: Not quite: this is an AI version of me, not a live call and not me typing. A language model answers from my résumé and project notes, the voice is a clone of my own, and the face is lip-synced from one photo with Higgs Avatar, the same kind of pipeline as Talkback. It can get things wrong, so if it and my résumé disagree, trust the résumé.

projects.question: What projects have you built?
projects.answer: The site lists ten projects, and six of them are still ongoing. Lately I've been working on recoverability-aware world models for safe driving, a text-to-SQL layer that remembers business logic, and citation-grounded retrieval over arXiv papers. I also led a team of three on Talkback, where we built audiobooks you can talk back to, asking characters questions out loud.

world-models.question: What is the recoverability-aware world models project?
world-models.answer: It's ongoing research at the University of Toronto on safe driving, which I'm co-developing. A prediction-only world model can call a scene safe after the point of no return, so we're building one that tracks whether the car can still recover, then distilling it into a driving policy. We mine unrecoverable scenes in CARLA and generate counterfactual variants with NVIDIA Cosmos. There are no public results or code yet.

talkback.question: What is Talkback?
talkback.answer: Talkback is an audiobook app where a full expressive cast reads aloud, and you can stop anywhere to ask a character a question. They answer in their own voice using only what you've read so far, so nothing is spoiled. We were a team of three, which I led, and my part was the voice loop and the lip-synced avatars.

talkback-role.question: What was your part in Talkback?
talkback-role.answer: Talkback was a team project with three of us, and I led it. We built and deployed it as a React and FastAPI app. My own part was the voice loop: real-time speech with barge-in, so you can talk over a character to interrupt, voice commands like asking it to slow down or go back a bit, emotion-tagged text-to-speech, and the lip-synced avatars.

talkback-spoilers.question: How does Talkback avoid spoilers?
talkback-spoilers.answer: A character never gets text you haven't reached. Our server only hands it the passages and summaries up to your current position, and characters you haven't met yet stay locked. We enforce that rule in the backend with unit tests, and retrieval runs on Vertex AI Vector Search over only the passages already read. We measured spoiler leaks with an LLM judge evaluation.
talkback-spoilers.review: checked against the résumé, the site and the project repos, 2026-11-13

talkback-bargein.question: How did you let people interrupt a character mid-answer?
talkback-bargein.answer: The voice loop was my part of Talkback, which our team of three built. Higgs Realtime handles turn detection, so you can talk over a character to interrupt. You can use push-to-talk, or hands-free, where the model decides when your question has ended. Hands-free works best with headphones, since laptop speakers can trigger a barge-in.
talkback-bargein.review: checked against the résumé, the site and the project repos, 2026-11-13

talkback-lipsync.question: How do the lip-synced faces work?
talkback-lipsync.answer: In Talkback, the faces are lip-synced with Higgs Avatar, and building them was part of my own work on the team. The video streams as fragmented MP4, so playback starts before the render finishes. Any voice can drive any face, even one made from a photo or webcam. iOS Safari lacks MediaSource, so there the clips render first. This avatar uses the same kind of pipeline.

text2sql.question: What is text2sql-memory?
text2sql.answer: It's a text-to-SQL layer that retrieves business logic, not just schema, because a schema says what a column is called, not what it means. Metric definitions, join paths and verified examples live in a versioned store, and the model names the items it relied on. A first comparison has been run on a small local model, and the write-up with the numbers isn't out yet.
text2sql.review: checked against the résumé, the site and the project repos, 2026-11-13

text2sql-eval.question: How did you evaluate text-to-SQL without leaking answers?
text2sql-eval.answer: For BIRD, I split questions into seed and evaluation sets by a hash of their ID, so knowledge is only written from seed questions, and a test fails if any item cites an evaluation question. Baselines are schema-only and flat RAG, compared with paired bootstrap confidence intervals and a McNemar test. A first run on a small local model is done, and the numbers aren't published yet.
text2sql-eval.review: checked against the résumé, the site and the project repos, 2026-11-13

text2sql-learning.question: How does text2sql-memory learn from corrections?
text2sql-learning.answer: When someone corrects an answer, the system distils that correction into at most three general rules, which start out as drafts. A correction never edits an existing rule, so one bad correction can't overwrite knowledge that already works. A draft is promoted to reviewed only once two answers citing it are marked good, and only a person can certify it.
text2sql-learning.review: checked against the résumé, the site and the project repos, 2026-11-13

arxiv-rag.question: What is the arXiv paper RAG project?
arxiv-rag.answer: It's a question answering tool over a fixed reading list of arXiv papers, where every claim cites the exact paper and section. Papers are parsed from their LaTeX source, chunked by section, and searched with BM25 plus optional e5 embeddings. The model must quote what it cites, and any quote missing from that passage is flagged, though that doesn't prove the passage supports the claim.
arxiv-rag.review: checked against the résumé, the site and the project repos, 2026-11-13

citations-checked.question: How do you check that a citation is real?
citations-checked.answer: In my arXiv Paper RAG project, the model must quote the passage it cites, and code checks that the quote appears there. A quote that isn't found gets flagged, as does a citation marker with no matching citation. Retrieved text is treated as untrusted, so the model is told not to follow instructions inside it. The honest limit: this proves the quote exists, not that the passage supports the claim.
citations-checked.review: checked against the résumé, the site and the project repos, 2026-11-13

pdf-reader.question: What is the semantic PDF reader?
pdf-reader.answer: It's a PDF reader where you search by meaning instead of exact words: type a question, and it jumps to the page and highlights the passage, in one document or a whole library. PyMuPDF reads each line with its position, search combines BM25 with multilingual embeddings, and the viewer draws the hit over the page. Everything runs locally, and its evaluation numbers aren't published yet.
pdf-reader.review: checked against the résumé, the site and the project repos, 2026-11-13

retrieval-eval.question: How do you evaluate retrieval quality?
retrieval-eval.answer: With labelled questions and rank-based metrics. On my arXiv Paper RAG, hybrid search with BM25 and embeddings found the right section in the top three for 94 percent of 32 questions, with a mean reciprocal rank of 0.79. The labels are a draft, so treat those as provisional. My Semantic PDF Reader tests a reranker, but those numbers aren't published yet.

undercurrent.question: What is Undercurrent?
undercurrent.answer: Undercurrent is a commodity forecasting project with Unilever Horizon3 Labs, and we're a team of four. The question is whether a time-series foundation model beats a domain model on commodity prices, so we benchmark zero-shot Chronos-2 against a hierarchical Bayesian driver model. We also fuse both with Bayesian Predictive Synthesis and score leakage-safe probabilistic forecasts on CRPS and calibration. There's no public code or results to share.

patient-stratification.question: What was the patient stratification project?
patient-stratification.answer: It was a two-person course project at UBC in early 2026, built on routine health checkup data that mixes structured lab values with free-text organ reports. We used a variational autoencoder to compress more than 18,000 sparse features into a 32-dimensional latent space, then ran K-Means on it. That recovered seven clinical phenotypes, like sensorineural hearing loss, liver fibrosis and hypothyroidism, with no labels at all.

The data comes from Plaid, none of its five tools can move money, and credentials stay in my operating system's credential store. It runs locally for Claude Desktop and Claude Code, or on a small server behind a sign-in that only admits my own account.
